title: Awards season is approaching. Will this queer Spanish epic upset ‘The Odyssey’?
content: In Christopher Nolan’s take on “ The Odyssey,” there are several nail-biting scenes in which Trojan soldiers face off against much larger foes, including a towering cyclops and an army of behemoth soldiers. Going into this awards season, “The Odyssey” is shaping up to be that giant, seen as the top contender for Oscar glory in several categories. Enter a potential giant-slayer. Hitting cinemas on Friday after a rhapsodic run at several major top film festivals, “La Bola Negra” may just be the film to finally win Netflix its long-coveted best picture prize. The streaming giant plans to run the Spanish film for 47 days in theaters prior to its digital platform debut — amounting to an unprecedently long cinematic runway for the company— in the hopes that the movie will charm audiences, critics and Oscar voters. Hollywood analysts believe “La Bola Negra” may be just the type of sweeping yet tender movie that might turn this awards season into a battle of David vs. Goliath. “I think they feel that this is as close as they’ve gotten to best picture, kind of maybe ever,” said Kyle Buchanan, the former awards season columnist for the New York Times set to launch his own podcast this month about Hollywood. “Certainly, ‘Roma’ won a lot of Oscars [in 2019], but I think that was a ‘head movie,’ and ‘heart movies’ typically are what prevail at the Oscars. They know they’ve got a ‘heart movie’ with ‘La Bola Negra.’” On paper, “The Odyssey” and “La Bola Negra” could not be more different. One is a mostly sexless , sword-and-sandal epic with a budget in the hundreds of millions (and a box office of more than $1.7 billion), stacked with top Hollywood stars and helmed by an already Oscar-winning director. The other is a subtitled work of queer yearning and romance made for under $17 million by two Spaniards (and a cast) who are all largely unknown outside their home country. (Glenn Close and Penélope Cruz pop up in smaller roles, with the latter almost stealing the movie in an unforgettable turn as an entertainer of the troops.) Still, industry observers think “La Bola Negra” may well have the juice needed to go all the way. Clayton Davis, chief awards editor at Variety, has predicted a nomination for the movie, writing that “‘La Bola Negra’ has the chance to rewrite Netflix’s Oscar history.” Similarly, Richard Lawson, former chief critic for Vanity Fair, has said the Spanish film is “right there in the frontrunner pack.” Directed by creative partners (and former romantic partners ) Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi (called ‘Los Javis’ in their native Spain and known to some Americans for their TV series “ Veneno ”), “La Bola Negra” weaves together three stories of queer identity connected to the Spanish Civil War. In the first, a teenage Carlos (Milo Quifes) in 1932 fails to gain membership into a social club, whose members vote against him using a blackball ballot system amid rumors of his homosexuality. In 1937, a young fascist conscript named Sebastián (the mononymous musician Guitarricadelafuente in his debut acting performance) is assigned to guard a wounded Republican prisoner of war (Miguel Bernardeau) to whom he begins feeling drawn. And in 2017, the directionless historian and former playwright Alberto (Carlos González) finds his life upended when he’s left a surprise inheritance from a grandfather he didn’t know he had. With shades of “Angels in America,” the movie is an ambitious and sumptuous portrait of identity, repression and what gets sacrificed in the long march of history. It’s not necessarily a love story between characters, but a love story to queerness itself. “What do we miss when we deny ourselves?” one character says towards the film’s almost fantastical ending. “Life.” Described by queer outlet Them as “one of the best LGBTQ+ movies of the century,” the film is inspired by the life and death of gay Spanish poet and playwright Federico García Lorca , who was murdered by fascist forces in 1936 and left behind an unfinished play called “La Bola Negra.” The movie’s 1937 storyline also draws on the 2013 play “La piedra oscura” by Alberto Conejero, with whom Los Javis share a screenwriting credit. In May, Los Javis shared the best director prize (along with the Polish filmmaker Paweł Pawlikowski, director of “Fatherland”) at the Cannes Film Festival, where the movie premiered to a 20-minute standing ovation and was swiftly scooped up by Netflix . Buchanan recalled covering the festival for the New York Times and “levitating” as he exited a screening of the movie: “Most people came out of that flush with excitement, faces red with tears, and just the feeling of, ‘Oh, finally . This is the movie of the festival, the movie that people are going to want to talk about, the movie that is definitely going to be a major player in the cinematic year.’” Since then, “La Bola Negra” has only gained speed as it rolled through other festivals, notching audience wins in San Sebastián and Toronto. The latter win bodes particularly well for Netflix’s Oscar hopes. Fourteen of the last 16 TIFF People’s Choice Award winners have scored an Academy Award nod for best picture, with four — “Nomadland,” “Green Book,” “12 Years a Slave” and “The King’s Speech” — claiming the top prize altogether. As Spain’s official entry in the international category at the Oscars, the film is favored to win that category, but it may well become the first foreign language movie since “Parasite” to take home the night’s top prize in 2020. With 10 Best Picture slots up for grabs, other buzzy films seem poised to join the final slate of nominees, like “ Project Haily Mary, ” “The Invite,” “Dune: Part Three” and “Wild Horse Nine,” a movie set for release in November and which stars John Malkovich as a dying CIA officer dispatched to Easter Island in the runup to Chile’s 1973 coup. Other wildcard movies could include “Artificial,” Luca Guadagnino’s movie on OpenAI, or even Nathan Fielder’s surreal documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, “You Can See Everything.” (Although it was dubbed “the movie of the year” by New York magazine , “You Can See Everything” still faces long odds as no documentary has ever been nominated in the top category.) Malkovich, a two-time Oscar nominee, is seen as an early favorite to win the best actor prize, although Andrew Scott in “Elsinore,” Robert Pattinson in “ Primetime ,” and Matt Damon in “The Odyssey” are all also on the hunt for their first acting wins. For best actress, analysts have positioned Julianne Moore as the odds-on favorite to take home a second Oscar for her turn in the comedy “The Debut,” in which she plays a meek mother who finds herself in the world of community theater. Inde Navarrette, star of the runaway hit “ Obsession ,” also seems poised to earn her first-ever nomination. The cast of “La Bola Negra” will all compete in the supporting categories, with Guitarricadelafuente and Cruz seen as the film’s best chances. Thanks to a recent change in Academy rules , Cruz could potentially be nominated twice in the same category, should voters want to also recognize her celebrated turn in “The Invite.” Buchanan said he expects Oscar voters will be charmed by the charisma of the “La Bola Negra” directors and ensemble when campaigning begins in earnest, but given Nolan’s stature in Hollywood and the enormous box office success of “The Odyssey” he believes the Spanish film remains an underdog. “It’s going to be hard to topple ‘The Odyssey,’ but what ‘La Bola Negra’ has a chance to do is rack up a lot of the same nominations and give that movie a run for its money in most categories — and eke out some of those wins,” he said.

title: Lena Dunham's Girls to return for limited HBO run
content:
HBO's award-winning show Girls will return to screens for a limited run ten years after the series finale aired.
Lena Dunham – the show's creator, writer, and one of its stars –  shared the announcement in a mock zoom call with members of the original cast Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke, Zosia Mamet and Andrew Rannells.
All five actors, whose careers launched off the back of Girls, will be part of the five-episode revival with production set to begin in 2027. Judd Apatow, who helped get the show green lit with HBO, will also return as executive producer.
"We always said we would only return to 'Girls' if there was a specific story we were burning to tell," Dunham said in a statement.
"I've missed these characters, but for a long time I couldn't quite picture them in the present day," she said.
"Then, right around my 40th birthday, they started talking to me in the shower. And, as you may remember, once this fivesome starts talking it's pretty hard to get them to stop," she said.
Girls, which ran for six seasons from 2012 to 2017, was nominated for 19 Emmys and won two, including best casting.
It follows the lives of four friends – Hannah, played by Dunham, Marnie, played by Williams, Jessa, played by Kirke and Shoshanna, played by Mamet – living in New York City during their 20s.
The show, created by Dunham when she was 23-years-old, attracted both praise and controversy during its airing. The BBC ranked it as number 30 on its 100 Greatest TV Shows of the 21st Century.
"We're thrilled to have Lena turn her gaze from the tumult of one's twenties to the milestone of turning forty," Amy Gravitt, executive vice-president of HBO programming, said.
"To say the world has changed since we last saw Hannah, Marnie, Shoshanna, Jessa, and Elijah is a massive understatement, but we know fans - old and new - will be happy to see how they've grown and relieved to see that they're still the 'Girls' we knew way back when."
The title of the limited run has yet to be announced, but Dunham did ask her fellow cast on the mock zoom call, "can we still call it Girls?", before joking "because we're old as".
Other cast and production members, most notably actor Adam Driver, were absent from HBO's official statement. Driver, in his breakout role, played Dunham's on-and-off again love interest in the show.
In her 2026 bestselling memoir Famesick, Dunham alleged Driver's on-set behaviour at times turned verbally aggressive and physically imposing. Driver has not publicly commented on the allegations.
In Famesick, Dunham also wrote about the breakdown of her working relationship and friendship with co-showrunner and executive producer Jenni Konner. Konner is not included in HBO's statement about the show's revival.
Dunham wrote on her Substack that "it's rare in life that you get the chance to return to something you love with new knowledge and a ... ton of gratitude.
"I love these girls (and boy) and I love all the people who have reminded us afresh why we do this, which is the joy of being together and the chance to wear yellow mesh…" she wrote.
Since Girls ended, Dunham has gone on to create the Netflix series Too Much in 2025 and indie film Sharp Stick.

title: Gavin and Stacey stars to feature in festive Julia Donaldson TV adaptation
content:
A new animated adaptation of a popular picture book to be aired over the Christmas period will be voiced by Welsh actor Rob Brydon and some of his Gavin and Stacey co-stars.
The Baddies, by children's author Dame Julia Donaldson and illustrator Axel Scheffler, tells the story of a troll, a ghost and a witch.
Brydon, as Ghost, will be joined by Sheridan Smith and Alison Steadman, who also starred alongside him in the popular sitcom, as well as Hammed Animashaun as Troll, Robyn Cara as Girl, and Francesca Mills as the narrator.
Previous adaptations of Dame Donaldson's books include The Gruffalo, Zog and The Scarecrows' Wedding, which also featured Brydon as scarecrow Reginald Rake.
The half-hour special celebrates courage, kindness and the power of standing up to bullies, according to the BBC and production company Magic Light Pictures.
It follows a girl with a blue spotty hanky who moves to a cottage near The Baddies.
A mouse then challenges the Baddies to see who can steal the hanky, but they soon learn that they may have met their match in the little girl.
"The Baddies was enormous fun to write because I loved inventing these gloriously wicked characters and then thinking about what might happen when they finally meet someone brave enough to outwit them," Donaldson said.
Sheridan Smith said it was "such a joy to be part of bringing The Baddies to life".
"The film is funny, spooky and full of heart, and the animation is absolutely beautiful. I think families are going to have enormous fun watching these wonderful characters causing chaos this Christmas," she said.
